## Why hypothesis testing exists

Imagine you run a coffee shop and someone tells you, "the new espresso
machine makes better lattes." You can't just take their word for it —
but you also can't test every possible latte forever. You need a
disciplined way to look at a limited amount of evidence and decide
whether it's convincing enough to change your mind about the world.

That, in one sentence, is what hypothesis testing is: **a structured
procedure for deciding whether the evidence you observed is surprising
enough, under a specific "boring" explanation, to abandon that boring
explanation.**

The "boring" explanation has a name: the **null hypothesis**, usually
written $H_0$. It's the default, skeptical,
nothing-interesting-is-happening claim — "the new machine is no better
than the old one." The competing, more interesting claim is the
**alternative hypothesis**, $H_1$ (or $H_A$) — "the new machine really
is better."

### The two ways to be wrong

Because we're making a decision under uncertainty, there are two
distinct ways things can go wrong:

|   | $H_0$ is actually true | $H_0$ is actually false |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **We reject** $H_0$ | Type I error (false alarm) | Correct decision (a "hit") |
| **We fail to reject** $H_0$ | Correct decision | Type II error (a miss) |

- A **Type I error** is convicting an innocent person — crying wolf.
- A **Type II error** is letting a guilty person go — missing a real
  effect.

There is an unavoidable tension here: if you make it harder to convict
(to protect innocent people), you will also let more guilty people go
free. You cannot drive both error rates to zero at once with a fixed
amount of evidence. Every hypothesis test is, in some sense, a
negotiation between these two risks.

We give the Type I error rate a special name and treat it as something
we control in advance: the **significance level**, $\alpha$. Setting
$\alpha = 0.05$ is a promise: "if the null hypothesis is really true,
I'm only willing to falsely reject it 5% of the time, in the long run,
across many hypothetical repetitions of this study."

The **p-value** is the probability, assuming $H_0$ is true, of seeing
evidence at least as extreme as what we actually observed. A small
p-value means "this would have been a weird thing to see if nothing
interesting were going on" — which is evidence (not proof) against
$H_0$. The p-value is **not** the probability that $H_0$ is true. It's
the probability of the *data* (or more extreme data), computed by
*assuming* $H_0$ is true. These sound similar but are logically very
different quantities — mixing them up is one of the most common errors
in applied statistics.

## How much can the data even tell you? — Fisher information

Before we can talk about good tests, it helps to have a sense of how
much a dataset can possibly tell you about an unknown quantity. This is
the intuitive role of **Fisher information**.

Think of it this way: suppose you're trying to estimate some unknown
parameter $\theta$. As $\theta$ changes, the probability of seeing your
particular data changes too. Fisher information measures how sharply the
probability of your data changes as you nudge $\theta$ around its true
value.

For example, imagine you're tuning an old analog radio dial to find a
station. Fisher information is like the sharpness of the signal peak: -
If the station comes in crystal-clear at exactly one dial position and
turns to static the instant you move the dial even slightly, the peak is
very sharp. It's easy to pin down the right setting precisely — this
corresponds to **high Fisher information**. - If the station sounds
almost equally decent across a wide range of dial positions, the peak is
flat. You could be off by a lot and barely notice — this corresponds to
**low Fisher information**.

A few consequences fall out of this picture almost for free, without
needing formulas:

- **More data generally means more (sharper) information.**
- **High Fisher information means your best possible estimate of**
  $\theta$ will be precise (a low-variance estimator is achievable). Low
  Fisher information means even your best estimator will be noisy. This
  relationship — more information caps how much uncertainty you're stuck
  with — is formalized by a result called the **Cramer–Rao bound**.
- **Fisher information also drives how good a hypothesis test can be.**
  A test is really just a decision built on top of an estimate. If the
  data barely distinguishes nearby values of $\theta$ (low information),
  it will also barely distinguish $H_0$ from a nearby $H_1$, and no
  clever test design can fix that — it's a property of the
  data-generating process itself, not of your method.

You don't need the formula to use this intuition, but for completeness:
Fisher information is formally defined as the expected curvature
(technically, the negative expected second derivative) of the
log-likelihood function around the true parameter value.

## What makes a test "best"? — Power

If we fix how many false alarms we're willing to tolerate ($\alpha$),
the natural next question is: **among all tests with that same
false-alarm rate, which one is best at catching real effects when they
exist?**

The probability that a test correctly rejects $H_0$ when $H_1$ is
actually true is called the test's **power**. Power isn't a single
number — it typically depends on how far the truth is from $H_0$. A test
might have great power for detecting a huge effect but poor power for
detecting a subtle one. This is usually visualized with a **power
curve**: power on the vertical axis, "true distance from $H_0$" on the
horizontal axis.

## A metal-detector analogy

Think of power like a metal detector at the beach.

- $\alpha$ is how sensitive you've set the machine to beep on plain sand
  (false alarms you've agreed to tolerate).
- Power is the probability it beeps when there really is a coin buried
  at some depth.
- A shallow coin (a big, obvious effect) is easy to detect — power near
  1.
- A deeply buried coin (a tiny, subtle effect) is hard to detect — power
  might be low even with a good machine.
- A bigger, more sensitive metal detector (more data, or less noisy
  measurements — i.e., **higher Fisher information**) raises the whole
  power curve.

### Uniformly Most Powerful (UMP) tests

A test is called **Uniformly Most Powerful (UMP)** at level $\alpha$ if
it has the highest possible power against *every single* alternative
value of $\theta$ simultaneously, among all tests with that same
$\alpha$.

The word "uniformly" is doing real work here — it means "no matter which
specific alternative you check against, this test wins (or ties)."
That's a very strong requirement:

A UMP test is is a remarkable, somewhat rare situation. It tends to
happen only in "nice," simple settings. A good example is when when
you're comparing one specific value of $\theta$ against alternatives
that all sit on one side of it (a **one-sided test**, e.g.,
$H_0: \theta \le \theta_0$ vs. $H_1: \theta > \theta_0$), in models with
a well-behaved structure (a **monotone likelihood ratio**).

When alternatives sit on both sides (a **two-sided test**,
$H_1: \theta \ne \theta_0$), a single test almost never dominates every
alternative in both directions at once. UMP tests generally fail to
exist in the two-sided case, which is why two-sided testing usually
settles for a good, sensible compromise test rather than a provably-best
one.

## The Neyman–Pearson Lemma (heuristically)

So how do you actually build a most-powerful test, at least when
comparing one simple hypothesis to another? This is exactly what the
**Neyman–Pearson Lemma** answers.

Suppose you must choose between exactly two fully specified
possibilities: $H_0: \theta = \theta_0$ versus $H_1: \theta = \theta_1$.
For any dataset you might observe, you can ask: "how much more likely is
this data under $H_1$ than under $H_0$?" That ratio is called the
**likelihood ratio**.

The Neyman–Pearson lemma says: **the best possible test is the one that
rejects** $H_0$ exactly when the evidence favors $H_1$ over $H_0$ by
more than some cutoff — i.e., rank every possible dataset by "how much
more $H_1$-like than $H_0$-like is it," and reject $H_0$ for the most
extreme, most $H_1$-favoring outcomes, until you've used up your
allotted false-alarm budget $\alpha$.

Why is this optimal, intuitively? Because you're spending your fixed
"false alarm budget" ($\alpha$) exactly where it buys the most power —
on the outcomes that are most diagnostic of $H_1$ over $H_0$. Any other
rule for deciding when to reject would, for the same $\alpha$, end up
flagging some outcomes that are less diagnostic while ignoring others
that are more diagnostic — leaving power on the table. It's the
statistical version of "spend your limited budget on the highest-value
evidence first."

This simple-versus-simple result is also the conceptual seed of UMP
tests: when a UMP test does exist (as in the one-sided, well-behaved
cases described above), it's usually because the likelihood-ratio test
from the Neyman–Pearson lemma turns out to be the same test, no matter
which specific alternative $\theta_1$ you plug in — so the one test
that's best against one alternative happens to be best against all of
them simultaneously.

## Putting it all together

In simple terms, here's what we've talked about today:

- **Fisher information** tells you the fundamental ceiling on how
  precisely your data can pin down an unknown parameter — the sharpness
  of the radio dial's peak.
- **Power** tells you how good a *specific test* is at detecting real
  effects, given that ceiling — how good your metal detector is at any
  given burial depth.
- **UMP tests** are the (rare, special-case) tests that are
  simultaneously the best metal detector at every possible depth.
- **The Neyman–Pearson lemma** tells you exactly how to build the best
  possible test when comparing two fully specified hypotheses — rank
  evidence by how much more it favors $H_1$ over $H_0$, and reject in
  the most favoring cases — and this same likelihood-ratio logic is the
  reason UMP tests exist at all in the one-sided cases where they do.

Everything so far has assumed that we get **one guess, made in advance,
checked once.** That's a much bigger assumption than it sounds like. The
rest of this lecture is about what happens when that assumption breaks —
which, in real research, is most of the time.

## The problem with asking too many questions

Let's say I hand you a coin and ask you to flip it 5 times. If it comes
up heads all 5 times, you win. Pretty unlikely — about a 3% chance.

Now here's a different game. I hand you 20 different coins, and you get
to flip each one 5 times. If *any single coin* comes up heads all 5
times, you win. Suddenly your odds of winning are much better — not
because any one coin got luckier, but because you gave luck 20 chances
to show up instead of one.

This is the whole idea behind the **multiple comparisons problem**, and
it's one of the most important ideas in this class: **the more things
you check, the more likely you are to stumble onto something that looks
meaningful purely by accident — even when nothing real is going on at
all.**

In research terms, a "5% chance of a false alarm" (that's what
$\alpha = 0.05$ means) sounds small and safe — for *one* test. But if a
study quietly runs 20 different tests and only publishes the one that
"worked," you're not looking at a 5%-risk finding anymore. You're
looking at something much closer to a coin flip's worth of risk that
it's a fluke, written out to look like a rare and exciting result.

**Why this matters in practice:** any time a study measures a *lot* of
things — dozens of outcomes, thousands of tiny regions of the brain,
hundreds of genes — and only reports the ones that "came out
significant," you should immediately ask: how many things did they check
in total, and did they account for that?

**How researchers try to fix it** — you don't need the formulas, just
the idea: - One approach is to say: "we want to be very sure we don't
get *even one* false alarm across the whole batch of tests" — and so we
make each individual test much stricter to compensate. This is like
raising the bar so high on every coin that beating it by luck alone
becomes rare even with 20 coins in play. - A different, more relaxed
approach is to say: "we're going to run a lot of tests, and we accept
that some fraction of our 'hits' will turn out to be false alarms — we
just want to know roughly what that fraction is, so we're not fooling
ourselves." This is common when you're deliberately doing a big fishing
expedition (like scanning thousands of genes) and a few false leads are
an acceptable cost of casting a wide net.

## Researcher degrees of freedom

Here's the twist that trips people up: you don't need to literally run
20 separate, clearly-labeled tests to fall into this trap. It can happen
invisibly, inside what looks like a single, honest study.

Imagine a researcher collects data and now has to make a bunch of small
decisions before they get their final result:

- Which of the several things they measured should they report as "the"
  outcome?
- Should they throw out a few weird data points, and by what rule?
- Should they check men and women separately? Younger and older
  participants separately?
- Should they keep collecting more data and peek at the result every few
  days, stopping as soon as it looks good?

None of these choices is dishonest on its own — they can all sound like
completely reasonable judgment calls. But each decision point is
secretly another coin flip. If the researcher (even without meaning to)
tends to make whichever choice makes the result look a little more
exciting, they've quietly run something like 20 hidden tests and just
shown you the one that worked — without ever calling it "20 tests."

**The fix**, in plain terms: decide your whole plan — what you're
measuring, how many people you'll test, which rules you'll use to
exclude data — *before* you ever look at the results, and then don't
deviate. Write it down publicly in advance (this is called
**pre-registration**). It's the equivalent of picking your path through
the maze with a blindfold on, before you can see which way looks shiny.

## "Significant" doesn't mean "big" or "important"

Statistical significance and practical importance are two different
questions, and a p-value only answers the first one. The p-value tells
you how surprising your data would be *if* $H_0$ were exactly true. It
says nothing about the magnitude of the effect itself.

The reason these come apart is sample size. A test statistic (like a
t-statistic) is roughly: **(observed effect) / (standard error of that
effect)**. Standard error shrinks as sample size grows — usually
proportional to $1/\sqrt{n}$. That means as $n$ increases, the
denominator keeps getting smaller, so even a fixed, tiny true effect
will eventually push the test statistic large enough to cross your
significance threshold. With enough data, you can get a significant
result for an effect too small to matter in any practical sense.
Conversely, with a small $n$, standard error is large, and even a
substantial true effect can fail to produce a significant result — a
Type II error driven by low power, not by the absence of a real effect.

This is why researchers report **effect size** alongside significance —
a standardized measure of *how large* the effect actually is,
independent of sample size. Common ones: - **Cohen's** $d$: the
difference between two group means, expressed in standard deviation
units. A $d$ of 0.2 is conventionally "small," 0.5 "medium," 0.8 "large"
— though these benchmarks are field-dependent and shouldn't be applied
blindly. - $r$ or $R^2$: for correlational or regression results, how
much of the variance is actually being explained.

A **confidence interval (CI)** carries more information than either a
p-value or a point estimate of effect size alone: it's a range of
values, computed from the data, such that (under repeated sampling) the
procedure would capture the true parameter a specified percentage of the
time — typically 95%. A narrow CI reflects a precise estimate; a wide
one reflects genuine uncertainty about the effect's magnitude, even if
the interval excludes zero. Two studies can report identical p-values
with very different CI widths, and the CI is usually the more
informative number of the two, since it directly conveys both the
estimated magnitude and the precision of that estimate.

## Why one significant result isn't the end of the story

A single significant finding is not, on its own, strong evidence of a
real effect, for the reasons already covered: it might be one
significant result out of many silently-run tests (multiple
comparisons), the one path through many researcher degrees of freedom,
or a real but practically negligible effect inflated in apparent
importance by a large $n$.

**Replication** is the mechanism the field relies on to sort signal from
noise. If an independent team, using a pre-registered design and new
data, reproduces a similar effect size and direction, that's
substantially stronger evidence than the original p-value alone —
because replication is largely immune to the failure modes above. A
fluke from multiple testing or a favorable path through researcher
degrees of freedom is very unlikely to reproduce consistently across
independent labs; a real effect, even a modest one, tends to.

A closely related issue is **publication bias**: significant, novel
findings are systematically more likely to be published than null
results, which biases the *visible* literature toward overestimating
both the prevalence and size of real effects. This is sometimes called
the **file-drawer problem** — the unpublished non-significant studies
sit in a file drawer rather than in a journal. Meta-analyses that
aggregate results across many studies attempt to correct for this (e.g.,
by testing for **funnel plot asymmetry**, a signature that small
non-significant studies are systematically missing from the published
record), but the underlying incentive — journals and researchers both
favoring exciting, significant results — remains a structural distortion
in how evidence accumulates.

**Takeaway:** a p-value alone is a thin basis for belief. A fuller
picture requires knowing how many hypotheses were tested, how much
analytic flexibility went into the result, the effect size and its
confidence interval, and — ideally — whether the finding has been
independently replicated.
